title: India Drops Pre-Defined OBC Lists From Census 2027, Reigniting Caste Data Debate
excerpt: The government will use open-ended caste entries instead of administrative OBC classifications, drawing fierce criticism from opposition parties who warn of a repeat of the unusable 2011 data.
body:
• India's government has dropped pre-defined Other Backward Class (OBC) lists from the Census 2027 caste enumeration, opting instead for open-ended text entries where respondents state their own caste.
  • The Registrar General's office argues OBC lists represent administrative "classes," not raw "castes," making them unsuitable for a door-to-door census exercise.
  • Critics warn the approach risks repeating the 2011 Socio-Economic and Caste Census failure, which produced 4.6 million unclassifiable caste entries and data the government itself called "unusable."
  • Enumeration has already begun in snow-bound areas as of September 1, 2026, with the full national count scheduled for February 2027.

India's decision to drop pre-defined Other Backward Class lists from the upcoming Census 2027 has reignited one of the country's most politically charged debates: how to count caste in a nation where social identity drives everything from college admissions to government jobs.

Instead of providing census enumerators with a master list of recognized OBC groups and a drop-down menu, field officers will record caste data through open-ended entries. Pre-defined categories will be limited to Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST), for which legally settled lists already exist. The decision has drawn fierce pushback from opposition parties, social justice advocates, and OBC groups who see it as a deliberate attempt to avoid producing accurate data on India's largest social bloc.

The 'Classes' vs. 'Castes' Distinction

Senior census officials defend the approach on constitutional grounds. The OBC lists maintained by the National Commission for Backward Classes comprise "Socially and Educationally Backward Classes" under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) of the Constitution — administrative groupings that aggregate multiple sub-castes, clans, and occupational groups under a single umbrella for affirmative action purposes, according to News Nest.

A single OBC entry in a state gazette may encompass dozens of distinct endogamous sub-groups using entirely different surnames across regions. When individuals identify themselves, they typically state their specific lineage or sub-caste — not the formal legal label assigned by a Backward Classes Commission. Census authorities argue that forcing a respondent to pick from an administrative list during a rapid door-to-door survey creates a mismatch between self-identity and legal classification.

The Federal Tangle

India does not possess a single, universally accepted catalog of OBCs. The Central OBC list contains roughly 2,483 entries, while each state maintains its own independent list. A community classified as OBC in one state may be categorized as Scheduled Caste in a neighboring state or listed under the general category elsewhere, according to the Registrar General's office.

The lists also include non-caste entries — "local borns" in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, tea garden workers in Assam — making them technically unsuitable as a uniform national drop-down menu, officials told the IAS Exam portal.

The 2011 Warning

The shadow of the 2011 Socio-Economic and Caste Census looms large over this decision. That exercise used a similar open-ended format and produced 4.6 million distinct caste names, sub-caste titles, synonyms, and phonetic misspellings — compared to just 4,147 caste entries recorded in the 1931 Census. The data was deemed so unusable that the government told the Supreme Court in 2021 that it was "inaccurate and unusable for any purpose whatsoever."

"The assessment recorded inside the Ministry is that the 2027 count is set to repeat the failure of the previous exercise."

— Civilsdaily, citing internal government assessment

The exercise cost approximately ₹4,900 crore. The caste data was never released.

Behind-the-Scenes Tussle

The decision was shaped by an unusual bureaucratic dispute. At a June meeting, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment offered to share its OBC list with the Registrar General's office for census purposes. But the initial draft minutes recorded a flat denial instead — stating that no such list existed and therefore pre-defined caste enumeration was not possible, according to Civilsdaily.

Ministry officials objected, arguing the onus for not using a pre-defined list was being shifted onto them. A revised note was submitted on June 11 and accepted on June 30. The episode exposed a deeper problem: two arms of government each own half the exercise, and neither is accountable for the output the other needs.

What's Next

Opposition leaders including the DMK's P. Wilson and activist Yogendra Yadav have warned that the roughly ₹12,800 crore being spent on Census 2027 will be wasted if the exercise is conducted without proper scientific planning. OBC groups have demanded unique caste coding and separate columns for OBCs and the General Category, mirroring the approach used for SCs and STs.

Enumeration has already begun in snow-bound regions as of September 1, 2026. The full national count is scheduled for February 2027, with March 1 as the reference date. The central question remains whether standardization rules for processing open-ended responses will be published before enumerators go into the field — or arrive only after the data is already in.
